content: Haloperidol, when used alone, is recommended as a treatment to manage aggression or agitation in individuals with psychosis. It is widely available and may be the only antipsychotic option in resource-limited settings. The purpose of this review was to evaluate whether haloperidol alone is effective in treating psychosis-induced aggression or agitation, particularly in situations where immediate intervention is necessary to prevent harm to the patient or others. The review involved a systematic search of the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group's Study-Based Register of Trials, which includes data from major databases such as AMED, BIOSIS, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, clinical trial registries, and other sources. The search was conducted without restrictions on language, date, document type, or publication status. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they involved individuals with psychosis-related aggression or agitation who were treated with haloperidol alone, administered by any route, and compared with other treatments. Outcomes of interest included the time to tranquillisation or sleep (within 30 minutes), the need for repeated tranquillisation within 24 hours, specific behaviors (e.g., threats or harm to self or others), and adverse effects. The review identified 41 studies, including nine new RCTs from the 2016 update. However, most studies were small, carried a high risk of bias, and did not reflect real-world clinical practice. The findings were as follows: 1. Haloperidol vs. Placebo: More individuals in the haloperidol group were asleep at two hours compared to placebo (2 RCTs, 220 participants; Risk Ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.82 to 0.95; very low-quality evidence). Dystonia was more common in the haloperidol group (2 RCTs, 207 participants; RR 7.49, 95% CI 0.93 to 60.21; very low-quality evidence). 2. Haloperidol vs. Aripiprazole: Fewer injections were required in the haloperidol group compared to the aripiprazole group (2 RCTs, 473 participants; RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.99; low-quality evidence). Dystonia was significantly more frequent in the haloperidol group (2 RCTs, 477 participants; RR 6.63, 95% CI 1.52 to 28.86; very low-quality evidence). 3. Haloperidol vs. Lorazepam: No significant differences were observed in the number of participants asleep at one hour (1 RCT, 60 participants; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.44; very low-quality evidence). The need for additional injections was also not significantly different (1 RCT, 66 participants; RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.43; very low-quality evidence). Adding lorazepam to haloperidol did not reduce adverse effects such as dystonia (1 RCT, 67 participants; RR 8.25, 95% CI 0.46 to 147.45; very low-quality evidence). 4. Haloperidol with Promethazine: More individuals in the haloperidol-alone group were not tranquil or asleep by 20 minutes compared to those receiving haloperidol with promethazine (1 RCT, 316 participants; RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.16; moderate-quality evidence). Acute dystonia was so frequent in the haloperidol-alone group that the trial was stopped early (1 RCT, 316 participants; RR 19.48, 95% CI 1.14 to 331.92; low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that while haloperidol alone may be life-saving in situations where no other options are available, its sole use in extreme emergencies could be considered unethical if alternative treatments exist. The addition of promethazine is supported by higher-quality evidence and appears to reduce adverse effects. The use of other antipsychotics is supported by limited and low-quality evidence. Adding benzodiazepines to haloperidol does not show strong evidence of benefit and may increase the risk of harm. Despite six decades of use, there remains a need for high-quality, independent trials that reflect real-world clinical practice.
